title: Sydney’s Road Stories

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Lines to regulate traffic were the first ‘statements’ to appear on Sydney’s paved roads. As motor vehicles became faster and the traffic became denser, the number of regulatory symbols grew. By the end of the twentieth century, the streets were covered with lines, signs, and sentences that road users needed to memorize. Today, traffic authorities are not the only ones to ‘write on the roadway.’ Many of the city’s population also regard the road as a giant billboard for announcements, private communications, slogans, jokes, and artwork. Their creative efforts mean that scanning the city’s streets has become a literary adventure.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Much of the writing on the road tells a story of struggle for territory and control. Between 1900 and 1930 the number of motorized vehicles on Sydney’s streets increased dramatically. Their speed meant that they were a danger to themselves, to pedestrians and to the horses they had begun to replace. To avoid harm, new road laws had to be introduced, warning signposts erected, and rules spelled out on the roadway. In the early days of street signs, the most common road marking to control these new vehicles was painted at intersections. These were first painted by hand, but in 1938 the New South Wales Department of Main Roads purchased a motorised line-striping machine from the California State Highway Department to make the process faster and more efficient. In the 1930s traffic authorities began using other kinds of road markers as well – metal studs, rubber pegs, and illuminated and reflective traffic domes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The proliferation of cars also meant greater demand for parking spots, and street signs also became necessary to indicate where cars could and could not park. In addition to parking signs, Sydney’s inner-city streets and back lanes are covered with many extravagant handmade signs homeowners have painted to defend access to their garages and driveways. The battle over territory is greatest where local attractions such as restaurants, sporting events, or concerts bring crowds of day (or night) trippers from outside the area.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Reminders of the dominance and danger of motorised vehicles can be read in the onsite markings that are methodically spray-painted by police at the scene of serious traffic accidents. Crash investigators returning to the site later use these patterns of angles and arrows to determine the causes of the accident. The diagrams remain long after the debris has been cleared away, serving as semi-permanent markers of ‘black spots’ on the road. Pedestrians are involved in accidents more often than motorists on Sydney roads, and traffic authorities try all sorts of tactics to remind people of this sobering fact. Some years ago, authorities launched a safety campaign whereby body outlines (like those painted at a crime scene) were stencilled at pedestrian danger spots.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Some remnant marks on the road are reminders of calamities, but others bring to mind celebratory times, such as the Sydney 2000 Olympic Games. A highlight event of the Games was the marathon, whose 42-kilometre route, marked with a blue line, wound through some of the city’s most attractive locations. The memory of Sydney’s hosting of the Olympics is still preserved on the streets by sections of the blue marathon line. Another souvenir of the Olympics is not generally recognised, but in 2000 ‘LOOK RIGHT’ stencils began appearing beside city kerbs as a warning to pedestrians. This measure anticipated the influx of overseas tourists needing to be reminded that vehicles in Australia drive on the left-hand side of the road.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Sydney loves a good party, and it is possible to find out what events are occurring by reading the road. Electronic road signs alert motorists to upcoming sports events, parades, and festivals, and of their corresponding traffic delays or road closures. But, more interesting, are signs which use the streets as free advertising space. Nightclubs sometimes use the city’s pedestrian crossings to advertise their ‘raves’. Until relatively recently, it was common to see hand-painted roadside signs (sometimes painted on a bed sheet and hung from a bridge or overpass) to welcome home a travelling relative or wish someone a happy birthday.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For many Sydneysiders* the street is not simply a thoroughfare but a publically available space for their own personal, political, or artistic statements. Written on the roadways are stories of democratic engagement, youthful exuberance, of romance, disappointment, and pain. Handmade works on the roadway are seldom produced impetuously; the act of creating them requires premeditation, planning, and physical daring. The reward for this effort can be an audience of thousands, although it is this same audience that will eventually wear the works away. Nevertheless, bold gestures like these demonstrate that the paved streets of Sydney have not been entirely ceded to the motor vehicle.

subtitle: Sydney, Australia’s oldest city, was settled by the British in 1788 without much planning. When Sydney’s first motor cars arrived at the beginning of the twentieth century, the city’s streets were sealed with tar, and their new hard surfaces lay like a page waiting to be written on
